notes.12:14: "A time and times and half a time" echoes Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 (three and a half years), corresponding to the 1,260 days mentioned in 12:6.
notes.12:18: The Saints Greek Critical Text reads third-person ἐστάθη ("he stood," referring to the dragon), whereas some later manuscripts read first-person ἐστάθην ("I stood," referring to John) and attach the clause to 13:1.
notes.13:1: The Greek text reads the singular "name of blasphemy" (onoma blasphemias) rather than the plural "names" found in some manuscripts.
notes.13:3: The Greek phrase "marveled after the beast" (ethaumasthe ... opiso tou theriou) is a pregnant construction expressing both amazement at the beast and following after it.
notes.13:8: The phrase "from the foundation of the world" follows "the Lamb who was slain" in the Greek word order, though it may modify either "was slain" or "has not been written" (compare Rev 17:8). The masculine pronoun auton (rendered "it") refers to the neuter "beast" according to sense.
notes.13:10: This textually complex verse has an elliptical first clause ("if anyone [is] for captivity, he goes away") and an active future verb in the second ("if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed"), whereas other manuscripts read passive forms emphasizing faithful endurance under persecution.
notes.13:18: The anarthrous Greek phrase "number of a human being" (arithmos anthropou) can mean either "a human number" (reckoned in human fashion) or "the number of a specific person." Some early manuscripts read "six hundred sixteen" instead of "six hundred sixty-six."
notes.14:3: The Greek text here reads "a new song" directly, without the comparative particle "as/like" (ὡς) present in some manuscripts.
notes.14:8: The Greek noun θυμός ("fury") carries the sense of both intense passion and fierce anger, forming a deliberate wordplay with "the wine of the fury of God" in 14:10.
notes.14:10: "Mixed undiluted" preserves the deliberate Greek oxymoron κεκερασμένου ἀκράτου: because ancient wine was ordinarily mixed with water, wine mixed at full strength signifies unmitigated divine judgment.
notes.14:12: The Greek genitive phrase τὴν πίστιν Ἰησοῦ ("the faith of Jesus") is grammatically ambiguous and may denote either faith placed in Jesus (objective genitive) or the faithfulness belonging to Jesus (subjective genitive).
notes.14:19: The Greek text pairs the feminine noun ληνόν ("winepress") with the masculine adjective τὸν μέγαν ("the great"), a grammatical irregularity characteristic of Revelation's style.
notes.14:20: One thousand six hundred stadia equals roughly 184 miles (about 296 kilometers), while the number itself (4 × 4 × 100) also functions symbolically to suggest complete extent.
notes.15:1: Greek ἐτελέσθη is literally past tense ("was completed"), a proleptic aorist depicting the completion of God's wrath through these final plagues as certain.
notes.15:2: Greek νικῶντας ἐκ ("conquering out of/from") is a compressed idiom conveying both victory over and deliverance from the beast; ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν may mean either "on" or "beside" the sea (echoing Israel at the Red Sea).
notes.15:3: Manuscripts vary between "King of the ages" (τῶν αἰώνων), "King of the nations" (τῶν ἐθνῶν), and later "King of the saints" (τῶν ἁγίων); the critical text reads "of the ages."
notes.15:4: The critical text has no explicit object ("You") after "fear" (φοβηθῇ), though some manuscripts add σε; ὅσιος ("holy") emphasizes God's devout purity and faithfulness.
notes.15:6: While an early textual variant reads λίθον ("stone," as in a precious stone), the critical text reads λίνον ("linen"), evoking priestly attire.
notes.16:3: Greek uses the neuter plural phrase "the things in the sea" (ta en te thalasse) in apposition to the feminine singular "every living creature" (pasa psyche zosa), a characteristic grammatical irregularity in Revelation.
notes.16:5: The divine title "the One who is and who was" omits the third element "and who is to come" (cf. Rev 1:4, 8; 4:8), signaling that the final judgment has now arrived.
notes.16:7: Literally "the altar saying"; the altar is personified as affirming God's righteous judgment (cf. Rev 6:9-10; 9:13).
notes.16:16: The Greek verb "gathered" (synegagen) is singular, regularly agreeing with the neuter plural subject "spirits" (vv. 13-14; cf. ekporeuetai in v. 14), though some interpreters take God as the implied subject. "Armageddon" (Harmagedon) is widely understood as a Greek transliteration of Hebrew Har Megiddo ("Mount Megiddo").
notes.16:21: A talent (talantiaia) weighed roughly 75 to 100 pounds (34 to 45 kilograms), emphasizing the catastrophic size of the hail.
notes.17:3: Greek en pneumati lacks the definite article ("in spirit" or "in the Spirit"), as in 1:10 and 4:2. The participles gemonta ("full of") and echon ("having") display Revelation's characteristic irregularity in gender and case when modifying the neuter noun therion ("beast").
notes.17:5: Greek mysterion ("a mystery") is punctuated here in apposition to "a name," reflecting the lowercase reading of the critical text; alternatively, it may be taken as the first word of the inscribed title itself ("Mystery, Babylon the Great...").
notes.17:8: The critical text reads the infinitive hypagein ("is about... to go") rather than the finite verb hypagei ("goes"). Greek parestai literally means "will be present" (or "will appear"), standing in direct contrast to "is not."
notes.17:9: The clause "and they are seven kings" appears at the end of verse 9 in the Greek text (placed in verse 10 in some translations) and can also be rendered "and there are seven kings."
notes.17:14: The final clause ("and those with Him...") has no explicit Greek verb; it may be read as an independent descriptive clause ("are called and chosen and faithful") or as a second subject sharing in the Lamb's victory.
notes.18:2: Greek phylake ("prison" or "haunt") can denote either a place of confinement for unclean spirits and birds or a desolate lair; some later manuscripts add a third clause mentioning "every unclean and hated beast."
notes.18:3: The critical Greek text reads peptokan ("have fallen"), supported by the earliest manuscripts, whereas some later manuscripts read pepokan ("have drunk"); Greek thymou can mean either "passion" or "wrath."
notes.18:13: Greek somaton literally means "bodies," a standard commercial term for slaves, paired climactically with psychas anthropon ("human souls" or "human lives," echoing Ezekiel 27:13).
notes.18:17: Greek pas ho epi topon pleon literally reads "everyone who sails to a place," referring to seafaring passengers traveling from port to port; later manuscripts read "all the company on ships."
notes.18:20: Greek ekrinen ho theos to krima hymon ex autes literally means "God has judged your judgment from her," an idiom indicating that God has vindicated His people by executing judgment against Babylon.
notes.19:6: The verb ἐβασίλευσεν ("has begun to reign") is an ingressive aorist, highlighting the decisive inauguration of God's universal reign rather than merely an ongoing state.
notes.19:10: The phrase τὴν μαρτυρίαν Ἰησοῦ ("the testimony of Jesus") is grammatically open to being read either as the testimony borne by Jesus (subjective genitive) or the testimony about Jesus (objective genitive).
notes.19:13: The source text reads βεβαμμένον ("dipped"), a notable textual variant where some manuscripts read a form of "sprinkled," likely under the influence of Isaiah 63:3.
notes.19:15: The verb ποιμανεῖ ("will shepherd") echoes Psalm 2:9 in the Septuagint, where shepherding with an iron rod represents stern, decisive authority over hostile nations.
notes.19:20: The Greek participle τῆς καιομένης ("that burns") appears in the feminine genitive rather than accusative, a grammatical irregularity typical of Revelation that links the burning directly to the lake of fire.
notes.20:4: The plural subject of "sat" is unspecified in Greek (echoing Daniel 7:9, 22), and "judgment" (krima) may denote either authority to judge or a favorable verdict granted to the saints. The aorist "came to life" (ezesan, literally "lived") is ingressive here and in v. 5, indicating a return to life, though interpreters debate whether it refers to bodily resurrection or spiritual vindication.
notes.20:5: A few manuscripts (including Codex Sinaiticus) omit the first sentence, likely due to scribal eye-skip between the repeated phrases "thousand years" in vv. 4 and 5, whereas the predominant manuscript tradition preserves it.
notes.20:9: Some later manuscripts add "from God" before "from heaven," but the earliest and most reliable Greek witnesses read simply "from heaven."
notes.20:12: "Books" (biblia) and "book" (biblion; also biblos in v. 15) may alternatively be rendered "scrolls" and "scroll." Some later manuscripts read "before God" rather than "before the throne."
notes.20:14: The final explanatory phrase "the lake of fire" is strongly supported by the earliest Greek witnesses, though it is omitted in many later manuscripts.
notes.21:3: The Greek reads the plural "peoples" (laoi) rather than singular "people" found in some later manuscripts, and ends at "with them" without the added clause "and will be their God."
notes.21:6: The Greek verb Gegonan is third-person plural ("They have come to pass"), referring back to the faithful words or decreed events; many later manuscripts harmonize it to the singular "It is done."
notes.21:10: The Greek phrase en pneumati lacks the article and may be rendered either "in the Spirit" (referring to the Holy Spirit) or "in spirit" (referring to a visionary state).
notes.21:16: Twelve thousand stadia is approximately 1,380 to 1,500 miles (about 2,200 kilometers), forming a massive cube of equal length, width, and height.
notes.21:17: One hundred forty-four cubits is approximately 216 feet (about 65 meters), based on a standard cubit of roughly 18 inches.
notes.21:18: The rare Greek term endomesis refers to the structure or building material of the wall.
notes.22:2: The phrase "in the middle of its street" can be punctuated with the river in v. 1 (as here, following the Greek punctuation) or with the tree of life in v. 2. The singular noun "tree" is used collectively to depict the tree of life lining both banks of the river.
notes.22:3: Greek katathema (a New Testament hapax) can mean either "curse" or "accursed thing" (cf. Zech 14:11). The singular pronouns "His" and "Him" refer jointly to God and the Lamb sharing one throne.
notes.22:7: The quotation shifts without a new introductory formula into the first-person voice of Christ ("I am coming quickly"), either spoken directly by Christ or relayed on His behalf by the angel speaking in v. 6.
notes.22:14: The earliest Greek manuscripts read "those who wash their robes," whereas later manuscripts and the Textus Receptus read "those who do His commandments," a variation aided by the close visual and phonetic similarity in Greek.
notes.22:19: Greek manuscripts read "the tree of life"; the reading "the book of life" in the Textus Receptus entered via a Latin copying confusion between ligno ("tree") and libro ("book").
notes.22:21: The earliest Greek text ends concisely with "with all"; later manuscripts expand the closing benediction to "with all the saints" or "with you all" and add "Amen."
